title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 35: Nasecore v. Energy Regulatory Commission: Publication of Applications for Rate Adjustments - an Indispensable Requirement of Due Process

primary_topics: Chapter 35 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Nasecore v. Energy Regulatory Commission, in which the Supreme Court en banc, through Justice Romeo S. Callejo Sr., unanimously held that the ERC gravely abused its discretion in approving Meralco's generation-charge increase without publication of the amended application.

The coverage holding: Section 4(e), Rule 3 of the IRR of the EPIRA speaks of any application or petition for rate adjustment or for any relief affecting the consumers without distinction, so it reaches an application under an adjustment mechanism like the GRAM and not merely an independent general rate application.

The second, independent ground: the GRAM Implementing Rules themselves were ineffective because they had never been published in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation as Executive Order No. 200 requires, nor filed with the Office of the National Administrative Register under the Administrative Code of 1987, following Tanada v. Tuvera.

The constitutional ordering announced on reconsideration: American case law on automatic fuel-cost adjustment clauses was unpersuasive absent textual similarity, and the Constitution recognized higher values than administrative economy, efficiency and efficacy when a procedure like the GRAM ran roughshod over the citizenry's right to due process.
sub_topics: The statutory setting: Republic Act No. 9136, the EPIRA of 2001, created the ERC in place of the Energy Regulatory Board and directed distribution utilities to file applications for the approval of their unbundled rates.

The ERC's March 20, 2003 Decision approved Meralco's unbundled rates but directed it to stop charging the Purchased Power Adjustment and to recover changes in purchased-power cost through the new Generation Rate Adjustment Mechanism instead.

The GRAM and ICERA: adopted by the ERC in its February 24, 2003 Order in ERC Case No. 2003-44 after consultations with utilities and consumer groups including Nasecore, they replaced the PPA and CERA and were made to take effect immediately.

The application at issue: in ERC Case No. 2004-112 Meralco sought to raise its generation charge from P3.1886 to P3.4664 per kWh under the GRAM formula, and the ERC's June 2, 2004 Order approved an increase to P3.3213 per kWh, effective immediately.

The petition: Nasecore and co-petitioners sought certiorari to nullify the June 2, 2004 Order, arguing that the lack of publication of the amended application deprived them of procedural due process under Section 4(e), Rule 3 of the IRR of the EPIRA.

The respondents' defense: Meralco and the ERC contended that the GRAM Implementing Rules, particularly Sections 2 and 5, radically differed from the IRR and did not require prior publication or solicitation of comments, the GRAM being an adjustment mechanism rather than an independent rate application.

The ruling on grave abuse of discretion: promulgated February 2, 2006 by the en banc through Justice Callejo, the unanimous Decision found that the amended application had never been published in a newspaper of general circulation, in violation of the IRR.

Why the rule covered the application: the IRR referred to any application or petition for rate adjustment or for any relief affecting the consumers without distinction, so it caught anything that would adjust the retail rate paid by end-users, whatever the component behind it, and Meralco's increase plainly raised consumers' costs.

The Freedom from Debt Coalition checklist: the Court recalled the six requirements of Section 4(e), Rule 3 -- verified application with proof of LGU receipt and certification of publication, a 30-day comment period, mandatory consideration of comments before any provisional adjustment, no hearing required on the provisional motion, resolution within 75 days, and a full-blown hearing within 30 days of the provisional order, limiting its life to 12 months.
The two innovations stressed: publication of the application itself rather than merely the ERC's notice of hearing, and the ERC's duty to consider the comments of customers and the LGU concerned.

The purpose of the requirements: protecting consumers and diminishing the disparity or imbalance between them and the utility, serving their right to due process while advancing people empowerment and consumer protection as EPIRA policy goals.

The consequence: the failure to publish was fatal, depriving consumers of the right to comment and of the chance to know the bases of the application so that they could contest the increase, while the ERC's power to grant provisional adjustments already answered Meralco's fear of a long and tedious recovery process.

The publication ground against the GRAM rules themselves: nothing showed that the rules in the February 24, 2003 Order had been published under Executive Order No. 200, and an ONAR certification of January 11, 2006 showed they had not been filed, so under Tanada v. Tuvera they had to be declared ineffective.

Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion concurring in the result: the publication requirement protects the public interest in transparent and reasonable electricity prices and applies indiscriminately to all petitions for rate adjustment, and under Freedom from Debt Coalition it is both jurisdictional and a component of procedural due process.

The Motions for Reconsideration: the ERC and Meralco, supported by intervenors PEPOA and PIPPA, argued from American case law that escalator and fuel-adjustment clauses required no notice and hearing, but the Resolution of August 16, 2006, again by Justice Callejo, unanimously upheld the Decision in toto and denied the motions with finality.

The reasons for denial: the cited American cases did not show that cost-recovery mechanisms were necessarily automatic or antithetical to notice and hearing, blind adherence was unwarranted without any showing of textual similarity between those statutes and the EPIRA, and logistical constraints could not outweigh the Bill of Rights.

notable_anecdotes: A rate increase effective immediately: the ERC's June 2, 2004 Order let Meralco's generation charge rise from P3.1886 to P3.3213 per kWh at once, without the consumers who would pay it ever seeing the application.

The rule that governed the rules: the Court found that the very GRAM Implementing Rules Meralco and the ERC relied on had themselves never been published or filed, a lapse documented by an ONAR certification dated January 11, 2006.

The consultation that proved nothing: the ERC had consulted consumer groups including Nasecore before adopting the GRAM, yet the mechanism it produced dispensed with publication of the very applications those consumers would have to contest.

The intervenors and the American authorities: PEPOA sought leave to intervene and PIPPA filed without leave, while the ERC and Meralco relied heavily on American case law on escalator clauses -- authorities the Court found did not even support their own theory.
The final word: the en banc denied the Motions for Reconsideration with finality on August 16, 2006, upholding the Decision in toto through the same ponente.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 35 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Nasecore v. Energy Regulatory Commission, decided unanimously by the Supreme Court en banc through Justice Romeo S. Callejo Sr. on February 2, 2006. Under the EPIRA of 2001 the ERC had approved Meralco's unbundled rates and ordered it to recover changes in purchased-power cost through a new Generation Rate Adjustment Mechanism, adopted with the ICERA in a February 2003 Order, in place of the old Purchased Power Adjustment. When Meralco applied under the GRAM to raise its generation charge and the ERC approved an increase from P3.1886 to P3.3213 per kWh effective immediately, consumer groups led by Nasecore sought certiorari, arguing that the amended application had never been published as Section 4(e), Rule 3 of the IRR of the EPIRA required. Meralco and the ERC answered that the GRAM rules radically differed from the IRR and required no publication, the GRAM being an adjustment mechanism rather than an independent rate application. The Court held that the ERC had gravely abused its discretion. The IRR spoke of any application or petition for rate adjustment or for any relief affecting the consumers without distinction, so it reached anything that would raise the retail rate; recalling the six requirements outlined in Freedom from Debt Coalition v. ERC, the Court stressed that the application itself, not merely the notice of hearing, had to be published, and that consumer and LGU comments had to be considered -- requirements aimed at protecting the consumers and diminishing the disparity or imbalance between them and the utility. The failure to publish was fatal, depriving consumers of the right to comment. A second ground was independent: the GRAM rules had themselves never been published under Executive Order No. 200 nor filed with the ONAR, and under Tanada v. Tuvera were ineffective. Justice Tinga concurred separately, calling publication both jurisdictional and a due-process component. On August 16, 2006 the en banc denied reconsideration with finality, rejecting American authorities on escalator clauses and holding that the Constitution recognized higher values than administrative economy, efficiency and efficacy.
